  "text": "In the spring, someone painted the harbour benches blue. Maren got paint on her coat and spent an afternoon working it out with a rag. A little remained at the cuff.

There were other changes. The baker retired. A boat came in with a name nobody liked, and by June everyone had stopped mentioning it. Erris grew too tall to swing her heels from the wall.

She still asked the time.

One evening Maren found her outside the lighthouse with a parcel under her arm.

"Mam says you'll want this."

It was a flask. The lid served as a cup.

"She says it keeps hot till morning."

Maren thanked her. She waited until the girl had gone before taking it upstairs.

After the three turns she poured some tea. It was too hot to drink. She stood holding the cup and watched a light move across the harbour. Someone was walking home along the opposite quay. The light disappeared behind the fish shed, then came out again.

She had never known what her mother did afterward. In all her remembering, Agnes was either climbing the stair or coming down. There must have been minutes like these. A cough. A loose thread pulled from a sleeve. Something warm held between both hands.

Maren drank her tea.

Before leaving, she opened the log and wrote beneath the date: West window needs putty.

At home she left the flask beside the sink. She would wash it in the morning. Through the open bedroom window came the knock of a halyard against a mast."

  "text": "By autumn the putty had hardened beneath Maren's thumb. She tested it whenever she passed the west window, though there was no reason to expect it to soften again.

Erris began bringing her schoolwork to the lighthouse. She sat at the little table below the clock, rubbing holes in the paper with her eraser. Maren learned to wind without disturbing the books.

One Thursday the girl asked what happened if she missed a night.

"I haven't," Maren said.

Erris waited, then bent over her figures.

That winter Maren caught a fever. From bed she heard the harbour clock strike seven, and later eight. Her coat hung from the door with its small blue stain. She tried to get up once.

In the morning the flask stood beside her bed. Under it lay a page torn from an exercise book.

Three turns. West window dry. Nothing else to report.

There was no signature. Maren read it twice, then slept until the room was dark.

When she returned to the lighthouse, the log lay open at the proper date. Erris had written in pencil, pressing hard. Maren ran a finger over the marks on the following page.

She left the entry as it was.

Outside, the tide was falling away from the steps. A length of weed caught on the lowest rail lifted and settled, lifted and settled. Maren watched until she was cold. Then she shut the window, checked the catch, and went downstairs, carrying the empty flask.

Halfway down she met Erris coming up.

They stood aside for each other."

  "text": "In March, Maren had a second key cut. The locksmith wrapped it in paper, though she had only to carry it across the street.

For several days it lay beside the bread bin. Then Erris came to return the flask, and Maren pushed the parcel towards her.

"The bottom lock sticks in wet weather."

"I know," Erris said.

There were evenings now when Maren stayed at home. She kept her hands occupied until the harbour clock struck, peeling potatoes long after she had enough. The strokes reached her unevenly across the roofs. Once she counted an extra one, but a pan had shifted on the hob, and she could not be certain.

She did not put on her coat.

At the lighthouse next morning, Erris had entered the wind and the height of the tide. Below these, in smaller writing, she had added: Someone on the steps before dawn.

Maren found the girl cleaning the lamp glass, though the lamp had not been lit in years.

"Did you open the door?"

Erris shook her head.

"Good."

She meant to say more. Instead she took the cloth and worked at a cloudy place the girl had missed.

Later, alone, Maren checked the tide tables. At the hour Erris had recorded, the steps would have been under water.

She set the book back on its shelf. Through the west window she could see the village washing lifting in the thin sunlight, her own blue-stained coat among it.

Before leaving, she laid a second dry cloth beside the lamp."
